Decision — email accounts live in settingsd, passwords in the app

Status: accepted 2026-10-16. Applies to the email app and the settings contract (email.*, contract 0.8.0).

The decision

  • Non-secret account settings live in settingsd.
    • The session profile's email group holds every account, in tree order: id, name, url, email, ca_path, enabled and signature. It also holds default_account and the mail options (page_size, mark_read_on_open, confirm_delete).
    • email.accounts is replaced whole by one fenced settings.apply. A change that removes the default account resets email.default_account in the same batch, so settingsd never holds half a change.
    • The email app follows the group through the session-profile summary and reconciles its connections live.
    • Ids are minted once (acct- and 12 hex digits) and never reused for another account.
  • Passwords never enter settingsd.
    • settingsd publishes retained snapshots on the Bus, which every client can read. The email group therefore has no password field, and every account record refuses unknown keys, so an apply carrying password is refused.
    • Each password lives in the email app's own file, <config>/secrets.conf.mix ({schema_version: 1, passwords: {id: …}}). The directory is 0700 and the file 0600, it is replaced atomically, and the poison-pill law applies: a malformed file is never overwritten.
    • Only the email app writes that file, and a password leaves it only toward the account's own server.
  • A password is reachable only through a write-only command.
    • email.account.password.set {id, password} stores a password and reconnects the account.
    • email.account.set may carry password too. It is held only once settingsd has accepted the account.
    • No command, topic, log line or diagnostic returns a password. email.accounts and email.info report has_password: bool.
  • Preferences is the configuration surface.
    • Accounts are added, edited, removed, reordered and made the default in Preferences' Email section, which writes email.* through settingsd. It sets passwords through email.account.password.set, starting Email first if it is not running.
    • The email app has no account form of its own. With no account, or with an account that failed or has no password, it offers Open Email Settings.
  • The app keeps a cache of the last accounts it read in its own config (schema 2, which holds no secret). When settingsd is absent, the cached accounts open read-only and the status line says so. Account writes are refused with UNAVAILABLE until settingsd is back.
  • The single account of an older install migrates once, losing nothing.
    • The account comes from the schema-1 config.conf.mix and is given an id derived from its URL and address.
    • Its password is written to the secrets file first. An inline CA bundle goes to a 0600 file beside it, which the account then names by ca_path.
    • The account is then applied to settingsd, and made the default when there is none. An account settingsd already holds with the same URL and address is adopted instead.
    • The schema-1 file is kept, and is written back unchanged, until settingsd has the account and its password is durable under that account's id. Only then is it rewritten as schema 2.

Why

  • The Bus must not carry secrets. The session profile is retained and broadcast so that any app can follow it. A password there would be readable by every Bus client and would appear in every snapshot and backup of the profile.
  • One place to configure. Terminal preferences already live in settingsd and are edited in Preferences. Mail accounts are the same kind of thing, and a second account form inside the app would drift from it.
  • Automation needs the accounts as data. An agent can list, add or disable an account through settings.apply or the email commands. It never handles a secret, unless it is the one supplying the password.

Consequences

  • A settings read never deletes a password. Only an explicit action through Email does: email.account.remove, or email.account.password.set with an empty password. An account removed elsewhere (in Preferences, by a reset) drops the app's client and view, and leaves its entry in the 0600 secrets file, unused. That is accepted: losing a password to a misread would be worse.
  • An empty account list is not a removal of them all. settingsd omits the group at its defaults, so an older settingsd, a reset and a profile without the group cannot be told apart. While accounts are shown, such a read keeps them (views, connections, passwords) with a status note, until a read lists accounts again or one is removed through Email.
  • Migration steps land in order, each durably. First the password is saved to the secrets file. Then the account is applied to settingsd. Then, if settingsd held it under another id, the password is saved under that id. Only then is the schema-1 file rewritten. A failure at any step, including a poison-pill refusal to write the secrets file, leaves the schema-1 file untouched, and the next launch runs the migration again.
  • A conflicting change (two writers at once) is refused by the fence. The email app reads again, retries a few times, and then reports CONFLICT.
  • MixOS has no keyring yet. The secrets file has the same trust as the app's other private files. A keyring, when it lands, replaces only that file; the settings group and the commands stay as they are.
